```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# HTML figures are drawn as PNG and kept as WebP: lossless (the same pixels in about half the space of PNG), or
# lossy at quality 90 when that is less than half the size, as for traces and densities of thousands of draws. The
# PDF figures stay vector graphics. Any failure of magick (not installed, no WebP, or a broken installation whose
# system libraries are missing) keeps the PNG
webp <- function(path) {
  if (knitr::is_latex_output() || !grepl(pattern = "[.]png$", x = path)) return(path)
  tryCatch(
      {
        if (!requireNamespace("magick", quietly = TRUE) || !isTRUE(magick::magick_config()$webp)) return(path)
        img <- magick::image_read(path)
        out <- sub(pattern = "[.]png$", replacement = ".webp", x = path)
        tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".webp")
        magick::image_write(
            image   = img
          , path    = out
          , format  = "webp"
          , quality = 100
          , defines = c(`webp:lossless` = "true")
          )
        magick::image_write(image = img, path = tmp, format = "webp", quality = 90)
        if (file.size(tmp) < file.size(out) / 2) file.copy(from = tmp, to = out, overwrite = TRUE)
        unlink(c(path, tmp))
        out
      }
    , error = function(e) path
    )
}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = FALSE, comment = "", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.8,
                      dev = if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "cairo_pdf" else "ragg_png", dpi = 96,
                      fig.process = webp)
if (requireNamespace("bayesammi", quietly = TRUE)) library(bayesammi) else
  pkgload::load_all(export_all = FALSE, helpers = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
```

# Abstract

A posterior sample answers the questions a breeder asks in probabilities: how likely is a genotype to be among the
best, how stable is it, and what yield can be expected in a cell that was never grown. This vignette goes through
`bam_superiority()`, `bam_ranks()`, `bam_stability()`, `bam_predict()` and `bam_winners()`, and through the model
choice tools `bam_compare()` and `bam_ppc()`.

```{r fit}
fit <-
  bayes_ammi(
      .data   = Maiz
    , .y      = y
    , .gen    = entry
    , .env    = site
    , .rep    = rep
    , .nIter  = 4000
    , .k      = 2
    , .burnin = 1000
    , .thin   = 1
    , .chains = 2
    , .priors = bam_priors(
          mu_mean     = 0
        , mu_var      = 1e+8
        , tau_mean    = 0
        , tau_var     = 1e+8
        , delta_mean  = 0
        , delta_var   = 1e+8
        , lambda_mean = 0
        , lambda_var  = 1e+8
        , nu          = 1
        , s2          = NULL
        )
    , .level  = 0.95
    , .seed   = 9
    , .align  = TRUE
    , .model  = "AMMI"
    , .het    = FALSE
    , .waic   = TRUE
    )
```

# Probabilities of superior performance and stability

Dias et al. (2022) select the best $s$ fraction of $G$ genotypes, that is $\lceil sG \rceil$ of them, in every
draw. Write $\bar{\eta}_{i\cdot}$ for the mean of genotype $i$ over the environments and
$\sigma^2_{GE,i} = \frac{1}{E}\sum_j(\eta_{ij} - \bar{\eta}_{i\cdot} - \bar{\eta}_{\cdot j} +
\bar{\eta}_{\cdot\cdot})^2$ for its interaction variance. Then

* the probability of superior performance is the share of draws in which $\bar{\eta}_{i\cdot}$ is among the
  best $\lceil sG \rceil$;
* the probability of superior stability is the share in which $\sigma^2_{GE,i}$ is among the smallest
  $\lceil sG \rceil$;
* the joint probability is their product;
* the conditional probability is the probability of superior performance within each environment;
* the pairwise probability is $P(\bar{\eta}_{i\cdot} > \bar{\eta}_{i'\cdot})$.

```{r sup}
sp <-
  bam_superiority(
      fit           = fit
    , .s            = 0.2
    , higher_better = TRUE
    )
sp
```

```{r sup-plots, fig.height = 4.4}
plot(x = sp, which = "marginal")
plot(x = sp, which = "pairwise")
```

```{r sup-cond, fig.height = 4.8}
plot(x = sp, which = "conditional")
```

# Posterior ranks

```{r ranks}
rk <-
  bam_ranks(
      fit           = fit
    , higher_better = TRUE
    , .env          = NULL
    )
rk
```

```{r ranks-plot, fig.height = 4.6}
plot(x = rk)
```

The tile of genotype $i$ and rank $r$ shows $P(\text{rank}_i = r)$. A rank interval that spans several places is
the honest answer to "which is second?". Ranks within one environment come from `.env`:

```{r ranks-env}
bam_ranks(
    fit           = fit
  , higher_better = TRUE
  , .env          = "12"
  )$summary[1:3]
```

# Bayesian stability

`bam_stability()` gives the posterior of two stability measures for every genotype: the interaction variance of
Shukla (1972), and the AMMI stability value of Purchase et al. (2000),
$$\mathrm{ASV}_i = \sqrt{\left(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}\,\lambda_1^{1/2}\alpha_{i1}\right)^2 +
(\lambda_2^{1/2}\alpha_{i2})^2}.$$
The weight $\lambda_1/\lambda_2$ becomes unstable when $\lambda_2$ is drawn near zero, so it is computed from the
posterior means of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, and the scores from each draw. The yield stability index (YSI) adds
the mean rank of the yield to the mean rank of the ASV; small is good.

```{r stab}
st <-
  bam_stability(
      fit           = fit
    , higher_better = TRUE
    )
st
```

```{r stab-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(x = st)
```

# Predictions

```{r pred}
pr <-
  bam_predict(
      fit    = fit
    , .level = 0.95
    )
pr$genotypes
```

```{r pred-plot, fig.height = 4.4}
plot(x = pr, which = "genotypes")
```

# Which genotype wins where

```{r win}
bam_winners(
    fit           = fit
  , higher_better = TRUE
  )$mega
```

# Model choice

## Information criteria

`bayes_ammi()` stores the deviance information criterion (DIC; Spiegelhalter et al. 2002) and the widely applicable
information criterion (WAIC; Watanabe 2010) of the observed plots. Both are computed while the chains run, so no
draws need to be kept. `bam_compare()` puts several fits side by side:

```{r compare}
fits <-
  lapply(
      X   = 1:3
    , FUN = function(K) {
        bayes_ammi(
            .data   = Maiz
          , .y      = y
          , .gen    = entry
          , .env    = site
          , .rep    = rep
          , .nIter  = 2000
          , .k      = K
          , .burnin = 500
          , .thin   = 1
          , .chains = 1
          , .priors = bam_priors(
                mu_mean     = 0
              , mu_var      = 1e+8
              , tau_mean    = 0
              , tau_var     = 1e+8
              , delta_mean  = 0
              , delta_var   = 1e+8
              , lambda_mean = 0
              , lambda_var  = 1e+8
              , nu          = 1
              , s2          = NULL
              )
          , .level  = 0.95
          , .seed   = 9
          , .align  = TRUE
          , .model  = "AMMI"
          , .het    = TRUE
          , .waic   = TRUE
          )
      }
    )
names(fits) <- paste0("K", 1:3)
cp <- do.call(what = bam_compare, args = fits)
cp
```

```{r compare-plot, fig.height = 3.6}
plot(x = cp)
```

```{r kk, include = FALSE}
t <- cp$table
```

WAIC estimates the deviance of new plots of the same genotypes and environments (Gelman et al. 2014). `se` is the
standard error of each WAIC; `dWAIC_se` is the standard error of the difference from the best model, computed from
the plot-by-plot differences, and is the one to use when comparing (Vehtari et al. 2017). Here `r t$model[1]` has the
smallest WAIC; `r t$model[2]` is `r round(t$dWAIC[2], 1)` above it, `r round(t$dWAIC[2] / t$dWAIC_se[2], 1)` standard
errors of the difference, and `r t$model[3]` is `r round(t$dWAIC[3], 1)` above
(`r round(t$dWAIC[3] / t$dWAIC_se[3], 1)` standard errors). The column `lambda_last_lower` adds the posterior view:
the HPD interval of the last singular value of `r t$model[1]` reaches down to `r signif(t$lambda_last_lower[1], 2)`,
so a term whose interval nearly reaches zero improves prediction little and is weakly supported. Prefer the simplest
model among those that the standard errors do not separate.

## Posterior predictive checks

`bam_ppc()` simulates replicated trials from the posterior and compares statistics of the data with their replicated
distribution (Gelman et al. 1996). A posterior predictive p-value near 0 or 1 marks a feature of the data the model
does not reproduce.

```{r ppc}
pp <-
  bam_ppc(
      fit    = fit
    , .draws = 500
    , .seed  = 2
    )
pp
```

```{r ppc-plot, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(x = pp)
```

# Working with posterior, bayesplot and coda

The draws convert to the formats of **posterior** and **coda**, so the plots of **bayesplot** apply:

```{r bayesplot, fig.height = 3.6}
dr <- posterior::as_draws_df(x = fit)
posterior::summarise_draws(.x = posterior::subset_draws(x = dr, variable = c("lambda[1]", "lambda[2]", "sigma2")))
bayesplot::mcmc_areas(x = fit$draws, pars = c("tau[4]", "tau[5]", "tau[6]"), prob = 0.95)
```

# Interpretation

```{r int}
bam_interpret(
    x             = sp
  , higher_better = TRUE
  , top           = 5
  )
bam_interpret(
    x             = st
  , higher_better = TRUE
  , top           = 5
  )
```
